back: Random motion, negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces, elastic collisions.

front: When do real gases deviate most?

back: 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ at 273 K and 100 kPa.
PV = nRT: Pa, m³, mol, K; R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ (fixed amount of gas, T in K).

front: Why do real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature?
back: High p: particles close, so their own volume is significant. Low T: particles slow, so intermolecular attractions become significant.
At constant T and n: p ∝ 1/V, so p₁V₁ = p₂V₂.
At constant p and n: V ∝ T (in K), so V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.
At constant V and n: p ∝ T (in K), so p₁/T₁ = p₂/T₂.

front: Shapes of p vs V and p vs 1/V graphs (constant T)?
back: p vs V: curve (inverse proportion). p vs 1/V: straight line through the origin.

front: V vs T graph at constant pressure?
back: Straight line; through the origin if T is in K. With T in °C it extrapolates to −273 °C at V = 0.
kPa × 10³ → Pa; dm³ × 10⁻³ → m³; cm³ × 10⁻⁶ → m³; °C + 273.15 → K.
Collisions of particles with the container walls; more frequent or more energetic collisions give higher pressure.

front: Compression factor pV/nRT for real gases?
back: Equals 1 for an ideal gas. < 1 when attractions dominate (moderate p, low T); > 1 when particle volume dominates (very high p).

front: Is 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ valid for liquids or at room temperature?
back: No. It applies only to (ideal) gases at STP: 273 K and 100 kPa. Otherwise use pV = nRT.
ρ = m/V = pM/RT — denser at higher pressure, lower temperature and higher molar mass.

front: Conditions where real gases behave most ideally?
back: High temperature and low pressure; small, non-polar molecules (e.g. He, H₂) behave most ideally.
